summary: Reports on the IAB workshop Show me the numbers: Workshop on Analyzing IETF Data (AID), held online from 29 November to 2 December 2021 and hosted by the IN-SIGHT.it project at the University of Amsterdam. It had two discussion parts with a hackathon between them, and summarizes the discussions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some researchers met online to talk about studying the IETF's own records, like emails and documents, as data. This is the meeting notes.

subtitle: How researchers are studying the IETF through its own data

tldr.problem: The IETF generates vast amounts of data about standards development—emails, RFCs, meeting records, participant information—but this resource is largely underutilized by researchers and the community itself.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB workshop convened researchers and IETF participants to share methods for analyzing IETF data, discuss what insights can be drawn, and identify open research questions around standards development, governance, and Internet evolution.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified five major research areas: data analysis methods, industry influence in standardization, community diversity and participation, the RFC publication process, and the environmental impact of IETF activities.

today: RFC 9307 is an Informational document describing the outcomes and research agenda from the November-December 2021 workshop. It remains a reference for researchers studying standards development and the IETF's internal processes.

sections.title: The Workshop and Its Purpose
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board convened the Workshop on Analyzing IETF Data (AID) in November and December 2021, bringing together researchers, IETF participants, and engineers. The workshop was hosted online by the IN-SIGHT.it project at the University of Amsterdam and ran as two discussion sessions separated by a hackathon.

The goal was to understand how IETF data is currently used, what insights researchers can draw from it, and what open questions remain about standards development. The workshop acknowledged that the IETF holds rich datasets—mailing list archives, RFCs, the datatracker with participant and meeting information, survey data, and website statistics—much of which is public but underutilized.
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers gathered online to talk about the IETF's records. They wanted to figure out how to study things like who writes the standards, how decisions get made, and whether the standards are fair and inclusive.

sections.title: Five Major Research Areas
sections.content:
The workshop organized discussions around five key topics. Tools, Data, and Methods covered the data sources available (mailing lists, RFCs, datatracker) and analysis tools developed by researchers. Observations on Affiliation and Industry Control examined how to track whether certain organizations dominate standardization decisions and how company mergers affect participation and leadership. Community and Diversity looked at who participates in the IETF and how to increase representation from underrepresented groups.

Publications, Process, and Decision Making addressed how to study the RFC publication process, measure standards success, and understand how the IETF makes decisions. Environmental Sustainability investigated the carbon footprint of IETF meetings and the extent to which protocols consider energy efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers split into five topics: how to get and study the data, whether big companies have too much power, how diverse the IETF is, how standards actually get approved, and whether the IETF cares about the environment.

sections.title: Understanding the Data Landscape
sections.content:
The workshop identified several key challenges in using IETF data. Data quality issues include inconsistent affiliation entries (people spell or capitalize their company names differently), making it hard to track company influence. There is no authoritative external source for tracking company mergers and acquisitions, so researchers must curate this data manually. Stream data—the continuity of email conversations—is fragmented across different systems as threads split, merge, and change.

The workshop also noted that the datatracker is a community tool that welcomes contributions and can be enhanced. Tools developed by researchers, such as BigBang and the ietfdata library, provide additional analytical capabilities. A data taxonomy was drafted to standardize how organization, participant, document, and meeting information should be structured for easier cross-organization comparisons in standards development research.
sections.plainLanguage: The data is messy. Company names are written in different ways, meetings move around the world in records, and emails get tangled together. But researchers have built tools to make sense of it, and the IETF tools can be improved.

sections.title: Studying Participation and Inclusion
sections.content:
A major concern at the workshop was understanding who participates in the IETF and ensuring the community is inclusive. Researchers discussed methods ranging from text mining and graph analysis to more human-centered approaches like surveys and interviews. The discussions acknowledged that defining diversity is complex—it might mean technical diversity across companies, geographic representation, or gender balance—and the goals of diversity affect how it should be measured.

The workshop highlighted that some groups are absent or underrepresented: women, network operators, and individuals from the African continent. The challenge extends beyond analysis—it requires understanding what drives people away and what makes them feel welcomed. The human element was emphasized: telling participants that their contributions matter is as important as the data itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Not everyone in the world can easily join the IETF. Some people don't know about it, some can't travel to meetings, and some don't feel welcomed. Researchers want to understand why and how to fix it by talking to people and studying the data.

sections.title: Standards Success and Decision Making
sections.content:
The workshop examined how to measure what makes a standard successful and how decisions are made in the IETF process. Questions included: What factors lead to an Internet-Draft becoming an RFC? How are RFCs used and referenced after publication? What determines whether a protocol is widely deployed? Researchers proposed studying these through analysis of email discussions, drafts, meeting minutes, GitHub activity, and external deployment data.

Understanding decision-making proved challenging because consensus is often implicit and decisions may not be explicitly recorded. The workshop identified the need to capture decision points early in the process and identify the factors that lead to effective decision-making. Some research investigated whether security concerns are discussed adequately during standards development and whether ambiguities in protocols can be detected computationally.
sections.plainLanguage: What makes one standard popular and another one forgotten? When does the IETF decide something, and how can we tell? Researchers want to study the emails and documents to answer these questions.

sections.title: IETF's Environmental Footprint
sections.content:
The workshop examined the IETF's environmental impact in two dimensions. First, researchers analyzed the carbon cost of IETF meetings themselves, considering participant travel, meeting locations, and the benefits of remote attendance. Initial results suggested that holding multiple in-person IETF meetings per year may be unsustainable in terms of carbon emissions. Second, the workshop studied whether Internet protocols themselves consider energy efficiency and climate impact during their design.

A review of RFCs from active working groups found limited consideration of climate change and energy efficiency topics. Only a small number of standards discussed these issues, even though energy consumption and environmental impact are increasingly important to Internet stakeholders. The workshop identified this as an open research area and an opportunity for the IETF to integrate sustainability into its standards work.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF asks people to fly to meetings all over the world, which produces a lot of carbon. Also, the network protocols it designs don't usually think about whether they save energy. The researchers looked at how much damage this does and how to improve it.
